title: Fall Concrete Sealing Checklist Before the First Salt
metaTitle: Fall Concrete Sealing Checklist Before Salt Season
metaDescription: Road salt and freeze-thaw cycles start early in Southwestern Ontario. Use this fall checklist to get your driveway, patio and walkways sealed before winter.
excerpt: Once road salt and freeze-thaw cycles start, unsealed concrete is already at risk. Here is a practical fall checklist for getting ahead of winter across Southwestern Ontario.

body.text: Southwestern Ontario's shift from fall to winter can happen faster than homeowners expect, and once road salt and freeze-thaw cycles begin, unsealed or under-protected concrete is already absorbing damage. Sealing works best when it is done with some lead time before winter conditions set in, both because the sealer needs time and the right temperature range to cure properly, and because crack repair and surface prep take longer than most homeowners assume. This checklist walks through what to look at and when to act, so a driveway, patio or walkway is protected before the first salt truck comes through.
Why timing matters more in fall than any other season

Acrylic and polyurethane sealers need a proper drying window to cure correctly, and cold, damp fall weather narrows that window as the season goes on. Sealing too close to the first hard frost risks a coating that has not fully cured before it faces its first freeze, which can affect how well it bonds and performs through the winter. This is different from spring or summer sealing, where warm, stable weather gives much more flexibility on timing. In fall, the practical goal is to get sealing done while daytime temperatures are still consistently mild and overnight lows are not yet dipping near freezing on a regular basis, which in most years across Southwestern Ontario means treating early-to-mid fall as the real window rather than waiting until late in the season.
Step one: walk the property and look for damage

Before scheduling anything, walk your driveway, patio, walkways and any pool deck or garage floor and look specifically for a few things: hairline cracks, especially near expansion joints and edges; discoloration or dullness where a previous sealer coat has worn thin; standing water that pools instead of draining after a rain; and any areas where the surface looks rougher or more porous than the rest. None of these are usually urgent on their own, but they are exactly the kind of damage that gets worse once salt and freeze-thaw cycling start, since water that gets into a crack and then freezes expands and widens that crack, a process that repeats and accelerates all winter if left unsealed.
Step two: prioritize surfaces that get salted

Not every surface on a property faces equal winter exposure. Driveways and front walkways almost always get salted, since they need to stay safe to walk and drive on through icy mornings, which makes them the highest-priority surfaces for fall sealing. Patios, pool decks and garage floors face less direct salt exposure but still deal with freeze-thaw cycling and, for garage floors, salt tracked in on tires and boots. If time or budget means sealing has to happen in stages, driveways and walkways are the logical first priority ahead of a winter that will bring regular salting, with patios and less-exposed surfaces following once the higher-traffic areas are covered. Details specific to driveways and walkways are at /services/driveway-sealing and /services/walkway-sealing.
Step three: handle crack and joint repair before, not after, sealing

It is a common misconception that sealer alone can bridge over an existing crack and stop the problem. Sealing over an unrepaired crack does not close it; water can still work its way in through the gap, and freeze-thaw cycling will keep widening it underneath the sealed surface, sometimes making the damage harder to see until it has progressed. Every job at All-Seal starts with thorough pressure washing followed by crack and joint repair where needed, and full drying, before any sealer goes down. Fall is the right time to have any visible cracking addressed properly rather than sealing around it and hoping it holds through winter.

items: Walk the property and note cracking, dullness, pooling water or rough patches
Prioritize driveways and walkways since these get salted first and most often
Have any cracks or joint gaps repaired before sealer is applied, not sealed over
Check whether existing sealer looks worn or is due for a fresh coat
Book a free inspection early in the fall rather than waiting for the first frost warning
Confirm anti-slip additive on any steps or areas prone to ice if that has not already been added

body.text: Step four: check whether existing sealer needs a refresh

Sealer protection generally lasts two to five years depending on traffic and exposure, which means a driveway sealed several winters ago may already be due for another coat even if there is no obvious damage yet. Wear shows up gradually, as a duller sheen, less water beading when it rains, or salt staining that used to wipe off more easily. If it has been a few years since the last application and the surface sees regular winter salt and plowing, fall is a sensible time to have it assessed rather than waiting for visible failure, since a worn coating offers progressively less protection even before it looks obviously bad.
Step five: think about anti-slip needs before ice season

If there are concrete steps, a sloped walkway, or an area near a pool that has felt slick in past winters, fall is the time to add an anti-slip additive rather than dealing with it mid-winter. The additive can be mixed into any sheen, high gloss, semi-gloss or matte, so it does not require compromising on how the surface looks. Steps in particular are worth a second look, since ice on stairs is a higher-consequence hazard than ice on a flat driveway, and the additive is standard practice on steps for exactly that reason.
Step six: book the inspection with real lead time

Fall is a busy season for concrete sealing across Southwestern Ontario, since a lot of homeowners are thinking about the same seasonal timing at once. Booking a free on-site inspection early in the fall, rather than waiting until the first frost warning shows up in the forecast, gives more flexibility on scheduling and more runway if crack repair or an old coating turns out to need more work than expected. Waiting until late in the season narrows the calendar and increases the chance that weather conditions push a job past the ideal curing window.
Once temperatures are consistently near freezing overnight, the window for a properly cured fall sealing job starts closing. Booking early keeps your options open.

None of these steps require special tools or expertise, just a walk around the property and an honest look at what condition the concrete is actually in heading into winter. faq.q: How late in the fall can concrete sealing still be done?
faq.a: It depends on the weather that particular year, since sealer needs proper drying and curing time before overnight temperatures consistently drop near freezing. Booking earlier in the fall gives more buffer than waiting until late in the season.

faq.q: Should I repair cracks myself before booking a sealing appointment?
faq.a: No. Crack and joint repair is part of the standard preparation process and is handled as part of the job, using pressure washing, repair and full drying before sealer is applied. There is no need to do this separately beforehand.

faq.q: Which surfaces should be sealed first if I can't do everything this fall?
faq.a: Driveways and front walkways are the highest priority since they get salted regularly through winter. Patios, garage floors and pool decks can often follow once the highest-traffic, most salt-exposed surfaces are covered.

faq.q: How do I know if my old sealer needs to be reapplied?
faq.a: Look for a duller sheen, less water beading when it rains, or salt staining that no longer wipes off easily. Since protection typically lasts two to five years, a driveway sealed several winters ago is worth having assessed.

faq.q: Can anti-slip additive be added during a fall sealing appointment?
faq.a: Yes. It can be mixed into any sheen and is commonly added to steps and areas near pools ahead of icy weather, without needing a separate visit.

faq.q: When should I book my fall inspection?
faq.a: As early in the fall as possible. This gives the most scheduling flexibility and the best chance of completing crack repair and sealing before overnight temperatures start dropping near freezing.
